title: Outcomes and surgical management of persistent fetal vasculature
condition_or_topic: Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) and its surgical management in children
clinical_background: PFV arises when embryonic ocular blood vessels fail to regress. It causes substantial visual impairment and accounts for 5% of childhood blindness in the USA. Most cases are unilateral and idiopathic, although rare familial bilateral cases have been linked to ATOH7 mutations, and bilateral PFV can occur with systemic syndromes. PFV is classified by anatomical location and severity. It often presents with leucocoria and microphthalmia; associated abnormalities and complications include cataract, retinal detachment, glaucoma and amblyopia. Management depends chiefly on the PFV subtype, while associated ocular disease and expected visual potential also inform the surgical decision. Mild cases with little obstruction of the visual axis may be observed, whereas cataract, posterior traction or more extensive disease may warrant surgery. The rarity of PFV has limited the size of studies evaluating outcomes.
objectives: To assess outcomes across the different forms of PFV.
To report the authors’ 9-year experience with predominantly surgical PFV management and evaluate visual outcomes.
clinical_question: In children with PFV (Patient), how do surgical approaches selected according to PFV type (Intervention), compared with observation or other surgical approaches used in the cohort (Comparator), relate to anatomical and visual outcomes (Outcome)?
interpretation: PFV classification and severity were central to surgical decisions and visual outcomes. Mild disease could sometimes be observed or treated with lensectomy or lens-sparing vitrectomy, whereas severe anterior or combined disease generally required both lensectomy and vitrectomy. In the authors’ experience, a coordinated combined procedure was the most effective approach for establishing vision in severe cases. Nevertheless, abnormal neuroretinal anatomy and complications, particularly retinal detachment and glaucoma, could limit the benefit of surgery. Among 11 eyes with severe combined PFV that underwent surgery, 10 had improved or stable vision at final follow-up; 1 had worse vision after an irreparable retinal detachment. The authors state that the outcomes of sequential surgery cannot be reliably compared with those of combined surgery in this series.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors describe their postoperative visual outcomes as comparable to prior surgical series involving at least 30 eyes with PFV, despite a higher mean age at surgery. Earlier reports also associated early intervention with better visual acuity and found a more favorable prognosis for isolated anterior PFV than for disease involving the posterior segment. The authors note that prior studies reported visual improvement after surgery for combined PFV, but did not provide enough outcomes by surgical approach to establish the relative effectiveness of coordinated combined surgery. Their rates of postoperative retinal complications and phthisis were similar to ranges reported in other studies, while their glaucoma rate was higher than in many published series; they suggest that differences in PFV severity might contribute, although the earlier reports lack details about the affected eyes. Prior studies found no difference in glaucoma rates between aphakic eyes with and without PFV. The authors also cite a study reporting lower success and more complications with Ahmed glaucoma drainage devices in PFV than in GCFS without PFV.
clinical_implications: A visually significant cataract or traction on the posterior pole can determine whether an eye with mild combined PFV needs surgery; some eyes need no PFV surgery because the findings have little visual significance or visual potential is poor.

Preserving the lens when there is no visually significant cataract avoids aphakic or pseudophakic anisometropia and loss of accommodation that can contribute to amblyopia. Astigmatic anisometropia can nevertheless persist after stalk segmentation.

In severe PFV, abnormalities of the macula and optic nerve, as well as retinal complications and glaucoma, restrict the visual prognosis and may necessitate additional operations. In the authors’ severe combined PFV groups, 57% (4/7 eyes) of observed eyes and 27% (3/11 eyes) of operated eyes could not detect light at final follow-up; these are outcomes of different clinical groups, not an established comparative effect of surgery.

The combined lensectomy-vitrectomy approach can preserve capsular support for a future IOL. Residual peripheral membranes and capsule can subsequently contract and contribute to pupil constriction, tractional retinal detachment, iris bombe or glaucoma.
Most affected eyes also need management of amblyopia and strabismus to maximize their visual potential.
practice_implications: Classify PFV by anatomical location and severity when selecting management, taking account of age, anticipated vision, ocular anatomy, initial vision, the fellow eye and parental wishes.

Consider observation for mild combined PFV with little visual obstruction or for severe disease with a closed funnel retinal detachment, severe optic hypoplasia and a normal fellow eye. The authors did not recommend surgery for 7 of the 18 eyes with severe combined PFV.

Consider lens-sparing vitrectomy when traction warrants treatment but the cataract is not visually significant; use lensectomy when cataract or a retrolental membrane obstructs the visual axis. Severe anterior and severe combined PFV typically call for both lensectomy and vitrectomy.

For severe cases undergoing surgery, the authors favor a coordinated approach involving paediatric anterior segment and retina specialists, with careful examination and treatment of peripheral retinal traction. They used endoscopic visualisation when posterior extension of a retrolental plaque was a concern.
Discuss the uncertain visual outcome and possible need for multiple operations thoroughly with parents before pursuing surgery for severe PFV.
Investigate systemic diagnoses and findings in the fellow eye even when PFV is unilateral.

Manage refractive error and amblyopia, including anisometropia that remains after surgery, and provide appropriate treatment for strabismus. Monitor operated eyes closely for retinal complications and glaucoma.
limitations: PFV severity differed among patients at presentation.
Although the study included 45 patients and 32 underwent PFV surgery, each surgical category contained few eyes.
strengths: The number of patients was relatively high for a rare condition.
open_questions: Whether PFV in the patient with mucopolysaccharidosis type VII was coincidental or related to fetal ocular glycosaminoglycan deposition remains uncertain.
No genetic mutations have been confirmed for MPCC; the authors identify a need to clarify this severe ocular abnormality.
The series cannot establish whether sequential lensectomy followed by vitrectomy produces worse anatomical or visual outcomes than a combined operation.
Prior reports do not provide enough outcomes by surgical approach to verify the effectiveness of coordinated combined surgery in severely affected eyes.
future_directions: Further study of coordinated combined lensectomy-vitrectomy is needed to verify its effectiveness in severe PFV.
Additional research is needed to determine effective glaucoma management in eyes with severe PFV.
A multicentre collaborative study could help address the small numbers associated with this rare condition, although the authors consider a larger prospective trial difficult.
study_design: Retrospective case series of children whose first presentation with persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) occurred between January 2011 and January 2020. The abstract describes the study as a retrospective cohort study.

population.description: Children younger than 18 years with PFV. The analysis included 46 eyes of 45 patients. PFV was clinically classified by location (anterior, posterior or combined anterior-posterior) and severity (mild or severe).
inclusion_criteria: PFV at initial presentation to the Kellogg Eye Center at the University of Michigan between January 2011 and January 2020.
Age younger than 18 years at initial presentation.
exclusion_criteria: PFV surgery performed outside the institution.
Age greater than 18 years at presentation.
Isolated Mittendorf dot or Bergmeister papilla.
population.mean_age: 16.7±31.3 months at presentation (median 2.8 months, range 0.7–138.0 months)
population.care_setting: Kellogg Eye Center at the University of Michigan, a university-based ophthalmology practice.

interventions: Observation without PFV surgery when an operation was not indicated.
Lensectomy, with or without intraocular lens (IOL) placement.
Combined lensectomy-vitrectomy, including removal of the retrolental plaque and separation of the stalk when present.
Postoperative refractive correction with a contact lens for aphakic eyes, or secondary IOL placement when a contact lens could not be tolerated and capsular support was adequate.
Part-time patching of the preferred eye for amblyopia; Atropine penalisation was used in some patients.
comparators: Eyes undergoing PFV surgery versus eyes managed without PFV surgery.
Outcomes by PFV location, severity and surgical approach.
Final optotype visual acuity in phakic eyes versus aphakic or pseudophakic eyes.

primary: Visual acuity at presentation and final follow-up, including improvement, stability or deterioration; the article does not formally designate a primary endpoint.
Anatomical status of the eye at the final visit; the article does not formally designate a primary endpoint.
secondary: Postoperative complications, including retinal detachment and glaucoma.
Additional retinal, glaucoma, anterior intraocular and strabismus surgeries.
Lens status, ocular findings and strabismus.

Optotype acuity assessed with Allen figures or Snellen in cooperative patients, typically aged 3 years or older, and expressed using LogMAR. For poorer or unmeasurable optotype acuity, assessments included detection of count fingers, hand motion or light; ocular preference was assessed with an induced tropia test using 10 base down prism, and aversion to light was assessed in infants younger than 3 months.

statistical_methods: Analyses used GraphPad Prism 8, Wilcoxon tests and Student’s t-tests. Reported p values were two-tailed, with <0.05 considered statistically significant. Stable visual acuity meant a change within one optotype line or no change in the ability to detect count fingers, hand motion or light; improvement or deterioration meant a change of two or more optotype lines or a change in those detection abilities.
follow_up: 32.6±29.8 months (range 1.0–108.8 months, median 22.5 months) at final follow-up.

main_findings.description: The analysis included children with persistent fetal vasculature (PFV).
main_findings.context: Initial presentations occurred between January 2011 and January 2020.

main_findings.description: Children generally presented early in life, although the ages varied widely.
Mild combined anterior-posterior PFV was the most frequent classification, followed by severe combined anterior-posterior PFV.
main_findings.context: Severe anterior PFV affected 3 eyes (7%); mild anterior and mild posterior PFV each affected 1 eye (2%).

main_findings.description: Most eyes received surgery directed at PFV.
main_findings.context: Surgery took place at a mean age of 10.1±20.9 months (median 2.4 months, range 0.7–101 months).

main_findings.description: The eyes that underwent PFV surgery received different initial procedures according to their ocular findings.
main_findings.value: 13 eyes (41% of 32 eyes) lensectomy alone; 11 eyes (34% of 32 eyes) combined lensectomy-vitrectomy; 3 eyes (9% of 32 eyes) sequential lensectomy then vitrectomy; 3 eyes (9% of 32 eyes) vitrectomy alone
main_findings.context: One eye (3% of 32 eyes) received lensectomy-IOL and one eye (3% of 32 eyes) received laser retinopexy. Combined lensectomy-vitrectomy was used for 3 eyes with severe anterior PFV and 8 eyes with severe combined anterior-posterior PFV. The Results text assigns all 13 lensectomies alone to mild combined PFV, whereas table 2 assigns 12 to mild combined PFV and 1 to mild anterior PFV.

main_findings.description: Some eyes were observed rather than undergoing PFV surgery because their visual potential was poor or PFV had little visual effect.
main_findings.context: Poor visual potential affected 9 eyes of eight patients, including 7 eyes with severe combined anterior-posterior PFV and extreme microphthalmia and/or chronic retinal detachment. PFV had insufficient visual impact to require surgery in 4 eyes with mild combined anterior-posterior PFV and 1 eye with mild posterior PFV.

notable_adverse_events: Additional retinal, glaucoma, other anterior intraocular or strabismus surgery was needed in 20 eyes of 20 patients, or 63% of the surgical cohort (20/32 patients), during follow-up; the reported number was 2.0±1.4 surgeries/eye (range 1–6, median 2).

Further vitrectomy was required in 5 eyes, or 16% of the surgical cohort (5/32 patients), after initial combined or sequential lensectomy-vitrectomy. Indications were retinal detachment in 3 eyes, retinal fold in 1 eye and cyclitic membrane in 1 eye. Further surgery occurred a mean of 14.9±24.2 months (range 1.2–58.1 months, median 5.4 months) after initial PFV surgery; the reported number was 1.6±0.5 vitrectomies/eye (range 1–2, median 2).

Postoperative retinal detachments or tractional folds requiring further vitrectomy developed in 16% of surgically treated eyes (5/32 eyes), all with severe PFV. Anatomy was successfully repaired and vision remained stable in 3 eyes; 2 eyes became phthisical. Another eye sustained an irreparable retinal detachment during its initial vitrectomy and later became phthisical.

Glaucoma was diagnosed in 20% (9/46) of eyes overall, including 25% (8/32 eyes) in the PFV surgery cohort and 7% (1/14 patients) in the observation cohort. The document uses different denominators for the latter comparison.

Glaucoma surgery was required in 6 eyes with prior PFV surgery, or 75% (6/8 patients) of those with glaucoma in the surgical cohort. Procedures occurred a mean of 33.4±39.1 months (range 4.4–105.7 months, median 39.5 months) after initial PFV surgery; the reported number was 2.0±0.6 glaucoma surgeries/eye (range 1–3, median 2).

Among the 9 eyes with glaucoma overall, 6 required surgery. Trabeculotomy controlled glaucoma in 1 eye with mild combined PFV. Eyes with severe PFV and glaucoma also had microphthalmia and required glaucoma drainage devices±cyclophotocoagulation for intraocular pressure control.

Additional anterior intraocular, non-glaucoma surgery was performed in 8 patients, at a reported 1.2±0.5 surgeries/eye (range 1–2, median 1). Indications or procedures included secondary IOL placement in 5 eyes, pupilloplasty/synechiolysis in 3 eyes, repeat posterior capsulotomy in 1 eye and attempted IOL placement in 1 eye.
Posterior capsular opacification, synechiae or membrane formation prompted surgery in 3 aphakic eyes; 1 pseudophakic eye required pupilloplasty.
Strabismus was present in 29 patients: 19 had esotropia and 10 had exotropia. Eye muscle surgery was performed in 9 patients, with 1.2±0.4 strabismus surgeries/patient (range 1–2, median 1).

subgroup_analyses: PFV classification comprised mild combined anterior-posterior disease in 23 eyes (50%), severe combined anterior-posterior disease in 18 eyes (39%), severe anterior disease in 3 eyes (7%), mild anterior disease in 1 eye (2%) and mild posterior disease in 1 eye (2%).

Table 2 assigns observation to 1 eye (100%) with mild posterior PFV, 6 eyes (26%) with mild combined PFV and 7 eyes (39%) with severe combined PFV. It assigns laser retinopexy to 1 eye (4%) with mild combined PFV; lensectomy to 1 eye (100%) with mild anterior and 12 eyes (52%) with mild combined PFV; lensectomy-IOL to 1 eye (4%) with mild combined PFV; vitrectomy to 3 eyes (13%) with mild combined PFV; sequential lensectomy then vitrectomy to 3 eyes (17%) with severe combined PFV; and combined lensectomy/vitrectomy to 3 eyes (100%) with severe anterior and 8 eyes (44%) with severe combined PFV.

Among eyes without PFV surgery, table 4 records stable vision in the 1 eye with mild posterior PFV; improved vision in 1 eye and stable vision in 5 eyes with mild combined PFV; and improved vision in 2 eyes, stable vision in 4 eyes and worse vision in 1 eye with severe combined PFV.

Among treated eyes, table 4 records improved vision after retinal laser in 1 eye with mild combined PFV; improved vision after lensectomy or lensectomy-IOL in 1 eye with mild anterior PFV and 9 eyes with mild combined PFV, with stable vision in another 4 mild combined eyes; improved vision after vitrectomy in 2 mild combined eyes and stable vision in 1; improved vision after sequential lensectomy then vitrectomy in 1 severe combined eye and worse vision in 2; and, after combined lensectomy/vitrectomy, improved vision in 3 severe anterior eyes and 4 severe combined eyes, stable vision in 3 severe combined eyes and worse vision in 1 severe combined eye.

Table 3 records glaucoma in 1 eye (0 requiring glaucoma surgery) among 7 observed eyes with severe combined PFV. Among surgically treated eyes it records glaucoma in 3 eyes (1 requiring surgery) with mild combined PFV, 1 eye (1 requiring surgery) with severe anterior PFV and 4 eyes (4 requiring surgery) with severe combined PFV.

Patients able to complete optotype testing at presentation were significantly older: 79.9±30.8 months (range 57.1–138 months), compared with 7.2±17.4 months (range 0.7–105 months) among the 40 patients unable to complete testing (p<0.0001).
Among 23 of the 32 eyes operated on before 6 months of age, final vision improved in 15, remained stable in 5 and worsened in 3. The article reports these counts descriptively.

The 3 phakic patients who underwent lens-sparing vitrectomy for mild combined anterior-posterior PFV had final visual acuities of 20/40–20/60. Among 14 eyes with mild combined anterior-posterior PFV treated by lensectomy±IOL, 3 attained 20/200 or better and 1 attained 20/40.

Of 3 eyes that underwent sequential lensectomy then vitrectomy after greater posterior involvement became apparent, 2 received vitrectomy within 2 weeks; the third received it over a year later after being lost to follow-up. At final follow-up, 2 of these eyes were phthisical. The authors state that their data do not establish whether sequential surgery had worse outcomes than combined surgery.
secondary_results: At presentation, 19 patients (42%) were women and 26 (58%) were men. Reported racial or ethnic groups were Caucasian for 33 patients (72%), African-American for 7 (15%), Asian for 4 (9%) and Hispanic for 1 (2%). The included eyes were evenly divided between right and left: 23 eyes each.
Cataract was present in 30 eyes (65%) and microphthalmia in 16 eyes (35%) at presentation.

Only 6 patients (6 eyes, 13%) completed optotype testing at presentation, with LogMAR 0.3±0.2 (range 0.2–0.7). Another 22 eyes of 22 patients were aversive to light; all were in patients under 11 months of age, including 16 under 3 months. Nine eyes of 9 patients were not aversive to light, while the contralateral eye was preferred in 7 patients by induced tropia testing. In each of the 2 patients with bilateral PFV, 1 eye was preferred by that test.

Two patients had bilateral PFV and confirmed genetic syndromes. Both eyes of the patient with mucopolysaccharidosis type VII (OMIM #253220) were included; only 1 eye of the patient with Microphthalmia, Syndrome 12 (OMIM #180220) and MPPC syndrome was included because the other eye had undergone initial surgery elsewhere.

Six patients with unilateral PFV had systemic congenital abnormalities. These included septo-optic dysplasia in 2 patients, both with contralateral optic nerve hypoplasia, and neurofibromatosis type 2 in 1 patient, who had bilateral combined retinal/retinal pigment epithelium hamartomas and an optic nerve glioma in the PFV eye. The fellow eye was normal in patients with Goldenhar syndrome, craniosynostosis or ventricular septal defect/dysmorphic features. Another patient without systemic abnormalities had MPCC syndrome in the PFV eye and contralateral optic nerve hypoplasia and chorioretinal coloboma; a further patient with unilateral PFV had retinopathy of prematurity previously treated with bilateral laser.

Among the 9 eyes with poor visual potential that did not undergo surgery, 2 had mild combined anterior-posterior PFV but vision was limited by corneal opacification associated with mucopolysaccharidosis type VII or by a retinal/retinal pigment epithelium combined hamartoma and optic nerve glioma associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

At final follow-up, 42 eyes of 42 patients were amblyopic in the setting of unilateral disease and had received part-time occlusion and/or atropine penalisation. The eye with mild posterior PFV was not amblyopic. Lens status across the cohort was aphakia in 22 eyes of 22 patients, IOLs in 6 eyes of 6 patients and phakia in 18 eyes of 17 patients. Of the phakic eyes, 14 had received no surgery, 1 laser retinopexy and 3 vitrectomy alone.

At final follow-up, 33 patients (34 eyes) could not complete optotype testing. Six eyes were aversive to light, 2 could count fingers at 4–8 inches and 18 eyes of 18 patients could fix and follow; 16 of those patients preferred the contralateral eye.

In a cited study, Soheilian et al reported an estimate for improved acuity in combined PFV of OR 7.9, p value =0.07; the present authors describe it as significant, although the reported p value is 0.07. In another cited study, Mittra et al reported that 71% of patients presenting with combined PFV improved to a final acuity of 20/300 or better. Neither result belongs to the present cohort.

scales_and_classifications.name: Persistent fetal vasculature classification
scales_and_classifications.description: Classifies PFV by anterior, posterior or combined anterior-posterior location and by mild or severe anatomical involvement.

scales_and_classifications.name: Isolated anterior
scales_and_classifications.description: PFV confined to anterior findings without a stalk or attachment to the posterior pole; severity depends in part on extension onto the ciliary processes.

scales_and_classifications.name: Isolated posterior
scales_and_classifications.description: PFV with a stalk or retinal fold but no attachment to the lens or ciliary processes; severity reflects optic nerve or macular distortion.

scales_and_classifications.name: Combined anterior-posterior
scales_and_classifications.description: PFV in which a stalk connects the posterior pole to a retrolental plaque; severity reflects distortion and anterior plaque extension.

scales_and_classifications.name: LogMAR
scales_and_classifications.description: Scale used for optotype visual acuity; poorer vision assessed by counting fingers, hand motion or light detection was not converted to this scale.

scales_and_classifications.name: Snellen
scales_and_classifications.description: One of the optotype methods attempted in cooperative patients.

scales_and_classifications.name: Allen figures
scales_and_classifications.description: One of the optotype methods attempted in cooperative patients.

scales_and_classifications.name: induced tropia test
scales_and_classifications.description: Test used to assess ocular preference in patients for whom optotype testing was unsuitable.

scales_and_classifications.name: SRK-T lens equation
scales_and_classifications.description: Equation used with surgical measurements to calculate IOL power.

scales_and_classifications.name: Teller acuity cards
scales_and_classifications.description: A visual acuity assessment named in the comparison of previous surgical series.

main_conclusion: PFV classification and visual potential should guide whether and how surgery is performed. Mild disease may be managed with lensectomy or vitrectomy alone, whereas severe disease generally requires both; in this series, a coordinated combined lensectomy-vitrectomy approach was the most effective approach used to establish vision in complex eyes. Retinal complications, glaucoma, amblyopia and strabismus remain important considerations.
narrative_summary:
This retrospective case series examined anatomical and visual outcomes in children presenting with PFV between January 2011 and January 2020. The analysis included 46 eyes of 45 patients, with a median presentation age of 2.8 months and median follow-up of 22.5 months. Mild combined anterior-posterior PFV was the largest category (23 eyes, 50%), followed by severe combined disease (18 eyes, 39%). Surgery for PFV was performed in 32 eyes (70% of 46 eyes); 14 eyes were observed because intervention was unnecessary or visual potential was poor.

At final follow-up, vision had improved or remained stable in 91% (42/46 eyes). In the surgical cohort, 66% (21/32 eyes) improved, 25% (8/32 eyes) remained stable and 9% (3/32 eyes) worsened. Five surgically treated eyes required additional vitrectomy, and glaucoma was diagnosed in 9 eyes overall, including 6 requiring surgery. Eight eyes could not detect light because of phthisis bulbi or optic nerve hypoplasia.

The authors emphasize assessing PFV location, severity and associated abnormalities before selecting an operation. Mild cases may permit observation or a single procedure, while severe anterior or combined disease often calls for coordinated lens removal and vitrectomy. They also stress postoperative surveillance and management of amblyopia and strabismus. Interpretation is limited by the retrospective design, variable severity and follow-up, lack of a control population, and small numbers within surgical categories.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Objective: assess outcomes across forms of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV). This retrospective cohort comprised children presenting to a university-based practice between 2011 and 2020; patients were excluded if surgery occurred elsewhere or follow-up was less than 1 month. Analyses used Wilcoxon and Student’s t-tests. The study included 46 eyes of 45 patients, presenting at 16.7±31.3 (median 2.8) months old and followed for 32.6±29.8 (median 22.5) months. PFV was mild combined anterior-posterior in 23 eyes (50%), severe combined anterior-posterior in 18 eyes (39%), severe anterior in 3 eyes (7%), mild anterior in 1 eye (2%) and posterior in 1 eye (2%). PFV correction was performed in 32 eyes (70%). Procedures included lensectomy in 13 mild combined eyes, vitrectomy in 3 mild combined eyes, sequential lensectomy then vitrectomy in 3 severe combined eyes, combined lensectomy-vitrectomy in 11 severe anterior or severe combined eyes, and laser retinopexy in 1 mild combined eye. An additional vitrectomy was needed in 5 eyes for retinal detachment, a fold or a cyclitic membrane. Glaucoma developed in 9 eyes; 6 required surgery to lower Intraocular pressure (IOP). At final follow-up, 32 eyes had at least form vision and 6 were aversive to light. Eight eyes, all with severe combined PFV, could not perceive light because of phthisis bulbi (7) or optic nerve hypoplasia (1); 4 of these eyes had not undergone PFV surgery. The authors conclude that PFV classification guides operative choice and that severe disease often calls for both lensectomy and vitrectomy to optimise anatomical and functional outcomes.

document_sections.heading: BACKGROUND
document_sections.content: PFV arises when embryonic ocular vessels fail to regress; it causes substantial visual impairment and accounts for 5% of childhood blindness in the USA. Most cases are idiopathic and unilateral, without an identified genetic cause. Rare familial, non-syndromic bilateral cases have been linked to autosomal recessive ATOH7 mutations. Bilateral PFV can occur with neurofibromatosis type 2, Aicardi syndrome, osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome, and chromosomal aneuploidies including trisomy 13, 15 and 18. Associations also include retinopathy of prematurity, Axenfeld-Rieger Syndrome and Peters Anomaly. PFV is categorised by anatomical site and severity and usually presents with leucocoria and microphthalmia. Other findings can include glaucoma, cataract, corneal opacification, coloboma, retinal folds or detachment, and spontaneous retinal or vitreous haemorrhage. PFV type principally guides surgery; coexisting ocular disease, expected visual potential, amblyopia and refractive needs also matter. Surgery seeks to restore anatomy, clear the visual axis, maximise vision and address complications. Observation can be suitable for mild combined anterior-posterior PFV with little pupillary obstruction. Severing the stalk between the posterior capsule and optic nerve by vitrectomy may improve function through axial growth and relief of posterior pole traction. Evidence for lens-sparing surgery is limited, although retaining the natural lens benefits amblyopia management in infants and young children. Lensectomy is standard when cataract or a retrolental membrane obstructs the visual axis. Earlier studies report a better prognosis for isolated anterior PFV than for posterior involvement because macular and optic nerve abnormalities are absent. In anterior disease extending onto and beyond the ciliary processes, concurrent or later core vitrectomy may reduce tractional retinal detachment risk, but access to a multidisciplinary surgical team can limit this approach. Isolated posterior disease often presents later; retinal traction or detachment may determine whether surgery is undertaken. Severe PFV, particularly with retinal detachment, has a poor visual prognosis, but surgery may help avert phthisis and glaucoma. Outcomes have generally improved with modern surgical technology, while disease rarity limits large studies. The authors aim to add their 9-year experience, predominantly involving surgery, and its visual outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Key messages What is already known about this subject?
document_sections.content: PFV is classified according to location and severity. Many affected eyes need surgery to improve their visual potential and lower the risk of complications such as retinal detachment and glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: What are the new findings?
document_sections.content: PFV category and severity influence both operative strategy and visual outcome. Mild disease may be observed or treated with lensectomy or lens-sparing vitrectomy. For severe anterior or combined anterior-posterior disease, the authors found combined lens extraction and full vitrectomy most effective for restoring anatomy and minimising complications.

document_sections.heading: How might these results change the focus of research or clinical practice?
document_sections.content: Management of these difficult cases depends on careful assessment of PFV category and severity. Collaboration between paediatric anterior- and posterior-segment surgeons was effective in establishing vision in severe disease.

document_sections.content: This table defines mild and severe isolated anterior, isolated posterior, and combined anterior-posterior PFV using retrolental plaque, ciliary-process extension, a stalk or retinal fold, and the degree of optic nerve or macular distortion. document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The authors describe a retrospective case series of children younger than 18 years whose first PFV presentation to the Kellogg Eye Center at the University of Michigan occurred between January 2011 and January 2020. Collected variables included age, gender, initial ocular findings, PFV type and visual acuity, follow-up duration, final anatomy and vision, intraocular and strabismus operations, operative dates and details, and postoperative complications. Cooperative patients, typically at least 3 years old, attempted Allen figures or Snellen optotype testing. Optotype acuity was converted to LogMAR; the stated equivalents for 20/200 and 20/20 were 1 and 0.1, respectively. Acuity worse than 20/400 was assessed through detection of count fingers, hand motion or light, without conversion to LogMAR. For patients older than 3 months and/or unable to cooperate with optotypes, ocular preference was assessed using an induced tropia test with a 10 base down prism. Infants younger than 3 months were assessed for light aversion because reliable fix-and-follow behaviour was not expected. Final acuity was considered stable if it remained within one optotype line or if the ability to detect count fingers, hand motion or light did not change. Improvement or deterioration required a change of two or more optotype lines or a change in those detection abilities. Exclusions were PFV surgery outside the institution, presentation after 18 years of age, follow-up shorter than 1 month, and an isolated Mittendorf dot or Bergmeister papilla. Clinical classification used anterior, posterior or combined anterior-posterior location and mild or severe disease. Every patient underwent examination under general anaesthesia at the first operation. Procedures used the Constellation Vitreoretinal Surgical System and varied with ocular pathology and surgeon preference. Lensectomy involved two 23-gauge limbal incisions, vitrector removal of the lens, opening of the posterior capsule and anterior hyaloid, and limited anterior vitrectomy. For IOL placement, intraoperative keratometry and axial length informed power calculation with the SRK-T lens equation; a foldable 3-piece MA60AC or single-piece SN60WF was selected according to sulcus or capsular position and inserted through a superior scleral tunnel. Lens-sparing vitrectomy used pars plana trocar positions according to the Lemley and Han nomogram. In aphakic eyes, trocars were placed immediately posterior to the limbus and the operation proceeded transpupillary through those cannulae. Combined lensectomy-vitrectomy used shared ports or incisions. Removal of the posterior capsule and retrolental plaque severed the stalk. Endodiathermy was infrequently required for bleeding hyaloidal vessels. Core vitrectomy included dissection of the posterior hyaloid and cortical vitreous by aspiration and/or manual peeling. With severe anterior involvement, a 19-gauge or 23-gauge endoscope helped visualise peripheral structures, identify posterior plaque extension and apply peripheral retinal photocoagulation when indicated. Aphakic eyes received contact lenses. The contact-lens refractive target below 2 years of age was −1.00 to −3.00; after 2 years, it was adjusted to plano, with glasses containing a +3.00 bifocal. If contact lenses could not be tolerated and capsular support was adequate, a secondary IOL was placed using an age-based refractive target. Patching the preferred eye was recommended for all patients with amblyopia, with daily duration determined by age and acuity. Some patients who did tolerate or were not compliant with patching received Atropine penalisation, as stated by the authors. Statistical analyses used GraphPad Prism 8, Wilcoxon and Student’s t-tests. Reported p values were two-tailed, and <0.05 was the significance threshold.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Forty-five patients first presented between January 2011 and January 2020. Presentation age was a median of 2.8 months, with mean 16.7±31.3 months and range 0.7–138.0 months. Nineteen patients (42%) were women and 26 (58%) were men; 33 (72%) were Caucasian, seven (15%) African-American, four (9%) Asian and one (2%) Hispanic. Two patients had bilateral PFV and confirmed genetic syndromes. Both eyes of a patient with mucopolysaccharidosis type VII (OMIM #253220) were analysed. For a patient with Microphthalmia, Syndrome 12 (OMIM #180220) and Microcornea, Posterior megalolenticonus, Persistent fetal vasculature and Coloboma (MPPC) syndrome, only one eye was included because the fellow eye had first been operated on elsewhere. Six patients with unilateral PFV had systemic congenital abnormalities. Two had septo-optic dysplasia and contralateral optic nerve hypoplasia. One had neurofibromatosis type 2, bilateral combined retina/retinal pigment epithelium hamartomas and an optic nerve glioma in the PFV eye. The fellow eyes were normal in three patients with Goldenhar syndrome, craniosynostosis, or ventricular septal defect/dysmorphic features. A patient without systemic abnormalities had MPCC syndrome in the PFV eye and contralateral optic nerve hypoplasia with chorioretinal coloboma. Another patient with unilateral PFV had retinopathy of prematurity treated with bilateral laser. Analysis included 46 eyes of 45 patients, with 23 right and 23 left eyes. Mild combined anterior-posterior PFV affected 23 eyes (50%), severe combined disease 18 (39%), severe anterior disease three (7%), mild anterior disease one (2%) and mild posterior disease one (2%). At presentation, cataract occurred in 30 eyes (65%) and microphthalmia in 16 (35%). Only six patients (six eyes, 13%) completed optotype testing initially, with LogMAR 0.3±0.2 and range 0.2–0.7. Twenty-two eyes of 22 patients were aversive to light; all were younger than 11 months, including 16 younger than 3 months. Nine eyes of nine patients were not light-aversive; seven eyes of seven patients showed preference for the fellow eye on induced tropia testing. In each of the two bilateral cases, one eye was preferred. Patients completing optotypes were significantly older, at 79.9±30.8 months (range 57.1–138 months, p<0.0001), than the 40 who could not, at 7.2±17.4 months (range 0.7–105 months). Fourteen eyes of 13 patients received no surgery. Nine eyes of eight patients had poor visual potential: seven had severe combined disease with extreme microphthalmia and/or chronic retinal detachment, and two had mild combined disease with vision limited by corneal opacification from mucopolysaccharidosis type VII or by a combined retina/retinal pigment epithelium hamartoma and optic nerve glioma associated with neurofibromatosis type 2. Intervention was unnecessary because PFV had minimal visual significance in four mild combined eyes of four patients and one mild posterior eye of one patient. PFV surgery was performed in 32 eyes (70% of 46 eyes) of 32 patients at mean age 10.1±20.9 months, median 2.4 months and range 0.7–101 months. Lensectomy alone was performed in 13 eyes (41% of 32 eyes), all in 13 patients with mild combined disease. Combined lensectomy-vitrectomy was performed in 11 eyes (34% of 32 eyes): three severe anterior and eight severe combined. Three severe combined eyes (9% of 32 eyes) received sequential lensectomy then vitrectomy, and three mild combined eyes (9% of 32 eyes) underwent vitrectomy alone. In mild combined disease, one eye (3% of 32 eyes) received lensectomy-IOL and another one eye (3% of 32 eyes) received laser retinopexy. During follow-up, 20 eyes of 20 patients—63% of the surgical cohort (20/32 patients)—needed further retinal, glaucoma, anterior intraocular or strabismus surgery; the number was 2.0±1.4 surgeries/eye, range 1–6 and median 2. Additional vitrectomy was required in five eyes, 16% of the surgical cohort (5/32 patients), after initial combined or sequential lensectomy-vitrectomy. There were 1.6±0.5 vitrectomies/eye, range 1–2 and median 2, for retinal detachment in three eyes, a retinal fold in one, and a cyclitic membrane in one. These procedures occurred an average of 14.9±24.2 months after initial PFV surgery, with range 1.2–58.1 months and median 5.4 months. Glaucoma was diagnosed in 25% (8/32 patients) of the surgical cohort versus 7% (1/14 patients) of the observation cohort. Six operated eyes, representing 75%, 6/8 patients with glaucoma in the surgical cohort, required glaucoma surgery for IOP control: 2.0±0.6 glaucoma surgeries/eye, range 1–3, median 2, at an average of 33.4±39.1 months after initial surgery, range 4.4–105.7 months and median 39.5 months. Eight patients underwent further non-glaucoma anterior intraocular surgery, averaging 1.2±0.5 surgeries/eye, range 1–2 and median 1. Indications comprised secondary IOL placement in five eyes, pupilloplasty/synechiolysis in three, repeat posterior capsulotomy in one and attempted IOL placement in one. Three aphakic eyes required operations for posterior capsular opacification, synechiae or membrane; one pseudophakic eye required pupilloplasty. Strabismus affected 29 patients—19 with esotropia and 10 with exotropia—and nine underwent eye-muscle surgery, at 1.2±0.4 strabismus surgeries/patient, range 1–2 and median 1. Final follow-up averaged 32.6±29.8 months, range 1.0–108.8 months and median 22.5 months. Forty-two eyes of 42 patients had amblyopia attributable to unilateral disease and had received part-time occlusion and/or atropine penalisation. One mild posterior eye had no amblyopia. In the bilateral mucopolysaccharidosis type VII case, neither eye was operated on and the preferred eye had milder PFV. In the bilateral microphthalmia syndrome 12 and MPCC case, only the preferred eye was included because initial surgery on the other eye occurred elsewhere. At the final visit, 22 eyes of 22 patients were aphakic, 6 eyes of 6 patients had IOLs and 18 eyes of 17 patients retained their lenses; among the latter, 14 had no operation, 1 had laser retinopexy and 3 had vitrectomy alone. Age, cooperation and vision level limited acuity measurement at both assessments. At final follow-up, 91% (42/46 eyes) had improved or stable acuity. Among operated eyes, 66% (21/32 eyes) improved, 25% (8/32 eyes) remained stable and 9% (3/32 eyes) worsened; the three worsening eyes developed irreparable retinal detachment and subsequently phthisis. Among eyes without PFV surgery, 21% (3/14 eyes) improved, 71% (10/14 eyes) were unchanged and 7% (1/14 eyes) worsened. Twelve eyes of 12 patients completed final optotype testing, with LogMAR 0.5±0.3, range 0.1–1.1 and median 0.3. Eight phakic eyes had LogMAR 0.3±0.1, significantly better (p=0.004) than the four eyes with LogMAR 0.8±0.4 that were aphakic (two eyes) or pseudophakic (two eyes). Thirty-three patients (34 eyes) could not complete optotypes. Six eyes were aversive to light; two could count fingers at 4–8 inches. Eighteen eyes of 18 patients could fix and follow, although 16 patients preferred the fellow eye. Eight eyes had no light perception because of phthisis bulbi following chronic retinal detachment (seven eye, as reported) or optic nerve hypoplasia (one eye).

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: PFV contributes substantially to childhood blindness through congenital anatomical abnormalities and subsequent retinal detachment, glaucoma and amblyopia. The authors examine medical and operative management and anatomical and functional outcomes over 9-year. Although over 90% of cases are sporadic and unilateral, bilateral disease is uncommon and usually accompanies genetic syndromes. Two patients (4%) in this series had bilateral PFV. One had mucopolysaccharidosis type VII, an exceptionally rare disorder caused by ß-glucuronidase deficiency that often results in prenatal or perinatal death. Because PFV had not previously been correlated with this disorder, the authors cannot establish whether their coexistence was incidental or reflected early fetal ocular glycosaminoglycan accumulation. The other bilateral patient had microphthalmia, syndrome 12, attributed to retinoic acid receptor beta mutations, as well as MPPC, described as a particularly severe combination of microphthalmia and PFV in which a posteriorly displaced lens fills most of the vitreous cavity. Another patient had unilateral MPPC, contralateral optic nerve hypoplasia and peripheral chorioretinal coloboma, without a systemic finding or genetic diagnosis to date. The authors state that no genetic mutations have been confirmed for MPCC and call for further investigation. Beyond these three cases, five patients with unilateral PFV had systemic findings: neurofibromatosis type 2, septo-optic dysplasia, Goldenhar syndrome, craniosynostosis or ventricular septal defect. Although many have previously been associated with PFV, the authors emphasise investigating systemic diagnoses and fellow-eye findings even when PFV is unilateral. Age, PFV type, macular abnormalities and optic nerve abnormalities inform the surgical decision and expected vision. Prior reports identified presentation age as an important visual-outcome predictor and associated early treatment with better acuity. In this cohort, mean surgical age was 10.1±20.9 months but median age was 2.4 months, within the stated critical visual-development period of 6–10 weeks. Among 23 of the 32 eyes operated on before 6 months, final vision improved in 15, remained stable in 5 and worsened in 3. Among the nine other operated eyes, two late-presenting patients aged 5 and 8 years had mild amblyopia and later underwent lens-sparing surgery for mild combined disease. Despite the higher mean surgical age, the authors consider their postoperative outcomes comparable to a small number of studies of at least 30 operated PFV eyes with mean operative ages of 2 to 3 months. Most cases in this and many earlier series had combined anterior and posterior involvement. In mild combined disease, a stalk produces minimal optic nerve distortion while reaching the posterior capsule. A visually significant cataract or posterior pole traction determined the need for surgery in this series: four eyes required none, three underwent lens-sparing vitrectomy for traction and one received laser retinopexy. Retaining a clear lens avoids aphakic or pseudophakic anisometropia and loss of accommodation that can promote amblyopia; the three phakic patients had final acuities of 20/40–20/60. Earlier lens-sparing series provided limited visual-outcome information because this subgroup was small. Stalk division does not eliminate possible astigmatic anisometropia from distortion of a non-cataractous lens, which must be managed to treat amblyopia. Mild combined PFV with visually significant cataract is commonly treated by lensectomy±IOL, and earlier literature generally describes favourable visual potential. Nevertheless, unilateral aphakia or pseudophakia strongly promotes amblyopia, requiring persistent treatment to reach 20/40 or better. In this series, 3 of 14 lensectomy±IOL eyes with mild combined disease attained 20/200 or better, and only one attained 20/40, in keeping with cited reports. Severe disease has anterior and posterior malformations that increase retinal and glaucoma risk; optic nerve and macular involvement further worsen outcomes. Electrophysiology has been used to estimate visual potential and identify eyes unlikely to benefit from surgery. The authors do not routinely obtain preoperative visual evoked potentials, citing possible inaccuracy from infant age and visual-system immaturity. Instead, severe-case decisions consider anatomy, initial vision, fellow-eye status and parental wishes. Observation can be considered for a closed funnel retinal detachment, severe optic hypoplasia and a normal fellow eye. Because the authors state that most untreated eyes eventually lose all vision through retinal detachment or glaucoma, they tend toward a more aggressive operative approach while discussing likely vision and repeat operations thoroughly with parents. Surgery was not recommended for 7 of 18 severe combined eyes. At final follow-up, 57% (4/7 eyes) of this observed subgroup had no light perception; three of these eyes (43%) had retinal-detachment-related phthisis. Among 11 operated severe combined eyes, 27% (3/11 eyes) had no light perception because of phthisis bulbi. Prior reports also described visual improvement after surgery for severe combined disease despite postoperative risks. Soheilian et al reported improvement in combined PFV (OR 7.9, p value =0.07), possibly related to anatomical retinal success, optical correction and amblyopia treatment; the reported p value warrants preserving the study's uncertainty. Mittra et al reported that 71% of patients with combined PFV improved to final acuity of 20/300 or better. Previous lensectomy±vitrectomy approaches through the pars plana or limbus produced modest outcomes. For severe anterior and severe combined PFV, the authors usually coordinated combined lensectomy-vitrectomy between paediatric anterior-segment and retinal surgeons: anterior lens removal preceded limbal vitrectomy, peripheral retinal examination and stalk division where needed. Other groups have used this approach. Retrolental plaques can extend past the ora serrata, producing peripheral retinal traction or detachment. Endoscopy helped assess posterior plaque extension and traction at the pars plana and pars plicata. When plaques extended posteriorly, they could drag the anterior retina and tent it over those structures. The authors state that endoscope-guided vitrectomy reduces iatrogenic breaks and retinal detachment during and after surgery, and permits far-peripheral photocoagulation around focal traction or defects when necessary. Inadequate peripheral examination and treatment predisposes to detachment complicated by retinal dialysis and proliferative vitreoretinopathy. Compared with pars plana lensectomy and vitrectomy, the coordinated approach often preserved capsular support for a future IOL. Close surveillance remains necessary because contraction of residual cyclitic or peripheral retinal membrane and capsule may constrict the pupil and sometimes produce tractional detachment, iris bombe or glaucoma. With the coordinated approach, 1 of 11 eyes lost vision because of irreparable detachment; the other 10 improved or remained stable. Prior series also used other techniques and did not provide sufficient approach-specific anatomical and visual outcomes. Further studies are needed to verify the coordinated strategy's effectiveness in establishing vision in severely affected eyes. Compared with staged lensectomy followed by vitrectomy, combined surgery reuses incisions or ports, causes less scarring and entails fewer general anaesthetics. The three sequential procedures here were unplanned: after lens removal, unexpectedly greater posterior involvement led to reclassification from mild to severe combined PFV. Two subsequent vitrectomies occurred within 2 weeks; another was delayed until over a year later after loss to follow-up. Two eyes ultimately became phthisical. Karacorlu et al likewise described seven eyes referred for vitrectomy after lensectomy, but did not report the interval or subgroup visual outcomes. Consequently, the authors cannot determine whether their staged approach produced worse anatomical or visual outcomes than combined surgery. Severe PFV can cause vision-threatening optic nerve and macular abnormalities, retinal folds and detachment; retinal complications are rare in mild anterior or mild combined disease. In this series, 16% of surgically treated eyes (5/32 eyes), all with severe disease, developed postoperative detachment or tractional folds requiring further vitrectomy. Anatomy was successfully restored and vision stayed stable in three; two became phthisical. A further eye sustained irreparable detachment during its initial vitrectomy and later became phthisical. Across cited studies, retinal complication and phthisis rates ranged from 5%–21% and 8%–23%, respectively, which the authors consider similar to their rates. They stress careful postoperative retinal monitoring. Glaucoma is an established PFV complication; early lens removal and congenital abnormalities can both contribute to elevated pressure. Glaucoma following cataract surgery (GFCS) is associated with early cataract extraction, particularly before 3 months of age. Earlier studies found no glaucoma-rate difference between aphakic eyes with and without PFV. Other work found medical therapy effective in over 50% eyes with GFCS, unlike primary congenital glaucoma, whereas angle surgery has lower success, likely reflecting distinct underlying pathology. Here, glaucoma occurred in 20% (9/46) eyes and more frequently after PFV surgery (25%, 8/32 eyes). This exceeds many published rates, perhaps because disease severity differed, although the cited reports do not specify which eyes developed high IOP. Six of nine glaucomatous eyes needed surgery. Trabeculotomy succeeded in one mild combined eye. Every eye with severe PFV and glaucoma also had microphthalmia and required glaucoma drainage devices±cyclophotocoagulation for IOP control. Few studies address PFV-associated glaucoma separately from GFCS. A cited recent study found Ahmed glaucoma drainage devices less successful and more complication-prone in PFV than in GCFS without PFV, using that latter acronym as printed. In this cohort, Baerveldt devices were used in four eyes and an Ahmed in one; further research is needed on glaucoma management in severe PFV. A strength is the relatively large patient group for a rare disorder. Declared limitations are retrospective case-series design, variable initial severity, unequal follow-up duration, no control population and small numbers per surgical category despite 45 included patients and 32 undergoing PFV surgery. A larger prospective trial would be difficult because PFV is rare; multicentre collaboration could address sample size. In conclusion, 70% of eyes received PFV surgery, but some did not need it because findings were not visually significant or visual potential was poor. For visually significant disease, classification is essential to choosing surgery. Mild disease may be managed with lensectomy or vitrectomy alone; severe disease generally needs both. The authors found coordinated combined lensectomy-vitrectomy most effective for establishing vision in complex cases. Abnormal neuroretinal anatomy and postoperative retinal detachment or glaucoma can limit results, particularly with marked posterior involvement. Most affected eyes also need suitable amblyopia and strabismus treatment to maximise vision. The findings are intended to support consultations with families and discussions of careful ongoing PFV management.

document_sections.heading: Table 5 Comparison of previous series analysing surgical management of PFV
document_sections.content: This table compares the current series with retrospective PFV surgical series by Sisk et al, Karacorlu et al, Tartarella et al and Hunt et al. It presents PFV distribution, procedures, surgical age, follow-up, lens status, vision before and after surgery, and postoperative complications. The authors use it to contextualise their outcomes and note that the earlier studies were retrospective.
